e.etymology: A respelling of Anniston or Aniston, known from Anniston, Alabama, a city whose name means 'Annie's Town', and from actress Jennifer Aniston. The -yn ending follows names like Paislyn.

assoc.t: Jennifer Aniston, Friends actress (sounds the same)

e.etymology: The Catalan form of Ramiro, a Visigothic name whose second element is mers, 'famous'; the first is read as 'counsel' or 'wedge'. In the US it sits close in sound to Amir and Jamir.
A modern American name that puts a Z in front of the sound of Jaylin and Kaylin, alongside Zayden and Zayne.
From the country, Old English Scotland, 'land of the Scots'. American parents began using it in the 2010s, mostly for girls, beside other place names such as Ireland and London.

assoc.t: Scotland, the country in the United Kingdom

e.note: Everyone will think of the country first.

e.etymology: An elaborate spelling of Brynlee, a modern American name that joins Brynn, from Welsh bryn, 'hill', to the -lee ending.
A spelling of Jonathan shaped by John, though the two names are unrelated. Jonathan is Hebrew Yehonatan, 'Yahweh has given', the son of King Saul and friend of David.
namesakes: Johnathon Schaech (That Thing You Do! actor)

e.etymology: A feminine form of Jan or a contraction of Johanna, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'; in English a modern variant of Jane. The same spelling is used for Arabic janna, 'paradise'.

assoc.t: Janna, wind mage in League of Legends

e.etymology: From Latin Sabina, 'a Sabine woman', the feminine of the Roman name Sabinus, after the Sabines, an ancient people of central Italy. Several early saints bore the name.
An anglicized form of the French surname de Chiel, carried by an old Maryland family. Crime writer Dashiell Hammett, whose mother was a Dashiell, made it known as a first name.
namesakes: Dashiell Hammett (author of The Maltese Falcon)

assoc.t: Dash Parr of The Incredibles, short for Dashiell

e.etymology: From Arabic iman, 'faith, belief', from the verb amana, 'to believe'. Eman is a common romanization of the name also written Iman. For boys it can also be a short form of Emmanuel.
From Hebrew li, 'to me', and or, 'light': 'my light' or 'I have light'. A modern Israeli name given to boys and girls; Liora and Leora are feminine forms.
A modern American coinage that joins the Ky- of Kylie and Kyla to the -lani ending of Hawaiian names such as Leilani and Kalani, where lani means 'sky, heaven'.
Short form of Clinton, an English surname taken from place names. Clint is also a Yorkshire village whose name comes from Old Danish klint, 'rocky hill'.

assoc.t: Clint Eastwood, actor and director of Westerns

e.note: In block capitals the L and I can run together, so CLINT may be misread as a vulgar word.

e.etymology: A respelling of Isabelle, the French form of Isabel, which grew out of Elisabeth in medieval Spain and southern France. Elisabeth comes from Hebrew Elisheva, 'my God is an oath'.
A modern American coinage, built on Zavier, a spelling of Xavier, with the -ion ending of names such as Davion and Javion.
From Irish Conán, 'little hound' or 'little wolf', from cú, 'hound', with a diminutive ending. Borne by early Irish saints and by a warrior of the Fianna in legend.

assoc.t: Conan O'Brien, late-night host known simply as Conan
Detective Conan, boy sleuth of Japanese manga and anime

e.etymology: From the place name: Lexington, Massachusetts, where the American Revolution began in 1775, and the towns named after it, including Lexington, Kentucky. In use as a first name since the 2000s, often for the nicknames Lex and Lexi.
From Arabic hiba, 'gift, present', from the verb wahaba, 'to give'. Often understood as a gift from God.
A modern American coinage: Gabriella without its G, or a blend of Abby with Briella. It carries no meaning of its own.
A respelling of Griffin, a medieval Latinized form of the Welsh name Gruffudd, whose second part means 'lord, prince'. Griffin is also the eagle-headed lion of legend.

assoc.t: griffin, the mythical beast that is part eagle, part lion
Gryffin, American DJ and electronic music producer

e.note: The y spelling recalls Gryffindor, the Hogwarts house in Harry Potter.

e.etymology: A modern name with no single source. It can extend Layan, an Arabic name meaning soft or gentle, or rework Leanna and Alayna around the popular Lay- sound.

e.meaning: halo of light around the moon
e.etymology: A respelling of Ayla. Turkish Ayla means the halo around the moon, from ay, 'moon'. Ayla is also a modern Hebrew name from elah, a terebinth or oak tree.
The form of Martha used in Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Polish and the Scandinavian languages, from Aramaic marta, 'lady, mistress'. In the Gospels Martha is the sister of Mary and Lazarus.
namesakes: Marta Vieira da Silva (Brazilian soccer great known as Marta)

assoc.t: MARTA, Atlanta's rail and bus transit system

e.etymology: A 20th-century coinage made popular by the Canadian R&B singer Tamia, whose hits of the late 1990s and early 2000s line up with the name's US peak in 2001.

assoc.t: Tamia, Canadian R&B singer known by her first name

e.etymology: A respelling of Carly, a feminine form of Carl that came into use in the later 20th century and also a pet form of Carla and Carlotta. Carl comes from Germanic karl, 'free man'.
A respelling of Kinley, a modern American first name taken from the surname Kinley or McKinley, Gaelic Mac Fhionnlaigh, 'son of Fionnlagh', a name meaning fair warrior.
A spelling of Zaida, the Spanish form of an Arabic name from the root for growth and increase, the feminine of Zayd. Zaida of Seville was an 11th-century Muslim princess at the court of Castile.
e.note: Sounds like zayde (also spelled zaida), the Yiddish word for grandfather.

e.etymology: A modern name used mostly in Central American and US Latino families, in the style of Spanish phonetic spellings of English names such as Keyla for Kayla and Keily for Kaylee.
The West African form of Muhammad, from Arabic for 'praiseworthy', by way of languages such as Hausa. It is one of the most common names in Senegal, Mali and Guinea.
e.note: In France the name has been used as a slur for men of African descent.

e.etymology: A respelling of Genevieve, the English form of French Geneviève, from the medieval name Genovefa. Its roots are uncertain, possibly Germanic words for kin and woman. Saint Genevieve is the patron of Paris.
The feminine of the Roman first name Caius or Gaius, whose meaning is uncertain; Roman brides spoke it in the vow 'where you are Gaius, I am Gaia'. In the US it is mostly a spelling of Kaia.
A modern name close in sound to Zayla and Layla. Its use rose after Zaila Avant-garde won the Scripps National Spelling Bee in 2021.
